To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Levin’s classification can be automatically learned from corpora, (2) the most effective feature sets are not based on alternation patterns, but rather on semantic similarities, and (3) the most effective features are simple co-occurrences.

1) Levin-style verb classification can be effectively performed using automatic methods; 2) the best-performing automatic classification systems do not use Levin’s features as their main source of information.

the question of how to build a robust and practically useful extension to Levin’s classes of verbs.

, although Levin-style verb classification is theoretically motivated and useful, the best performing automatic classifiers do not use the features most directly motivated by Levin’s work.

the best features are not the most informative, nor the most theoretically credible, but the most effective.

the best features for automatic verb classifications are not the same as the features that are most theoretically motivated.

Levin’s classes are not the best feature space to be used for automatic verb classification and the most effective features for automatic classification are based on dependency information and simple lexical co-occurrence information.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for automatic classification, Levin’s classes are best seen as a useful starting point rather than an optimal solution.
the theoretical motivations of Levin’s classes are only one of several factors which influence the effectiveness of a feature set.
